newsitem.title: USA: WORLD BONDS - Plucking Denmark from EU smorgasbord.
newsitem.headline: WORLD BONDS - Plucking Denmark from EU smorgasbord.

text.p: Danish governments bonds, with their currency stability and generous spreads over Bunds, continue to offer good value to investors seeking shelter from the vicissitudes of European Monetary Union, analysts said.
Denmark's robust economic fundamentals qualify it, along with Ireland and Luxembourg, to join a single European currency by meeting strict Maastricht convergence criteria.
However, Denmark's 1993 EMU opt-out provision gives Danish government bonds something of a safe-haven status in the runup to monetary union in 1999, analysts said.

"One of the things we've been looking for is for Denmark to outperform other European countries given its fundamentals," said Julie Grandstaff, vice president of global fixed income at Bailard, Biehl and Kaiser.
The Danish ten-year government bond has maintained a spread of 90 to 100 basis points over its German counterpart over the past several weeks, she said.
"In terms of the yield curve, certainly the ten-year sector would do well. The current spread there is about 97 basis points with a yield of 7.13 percent," she said.
Denmark's low inflation rate -- about 2.0 percent -- suggests a net yield of about 50 basis points over German Bunds, she added.

With a projected 1996 budget gap of 1.7 percent of gross domestic product compared with an EMU target of 3.0 percent, Denmark meets most of the EMU convergence targets, said Marc Chandler, senior currency analyst at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell.
"Their budget deficit as a percentage of GDP is among the lowest in Europe," he said.

Giving Danish bonds added appeal is the fact that the Danish currency has remained within a stable, narrow band against the German mark, helping to limit currency risk, said Michael Perelstein, managing director at MacKay Shields.
The crown has traded as low as 3.87 against the mark in recent weeks, but has generally maintained a level around 3.85 in the recent past, analysts said.
"It's basically like saying Denmark is like a sector in the German bond market that pays 90 (basis points) over comparable German governments, so it becomes a real buy," Perelstein said.
Analysts said the crown's low volatility appeals to investors looking to trade in interest rate differentials, selling marks and buying Danish paper.
Denmark initially rejected the Maastricht Treaty in an historic "no" vote in a referendum in June 1992.
It later voted narrowly in favor of the accord but only after the Danish government secured special opt-out provisions on monetary union and other key clauses.
"The European Union has said three countries meet the Maastricht criteria. Denmark is one of them, but their political will is questionable," Chandler said.
Executives of Denmark's two largest banks said earlier this week that Denmark's opt-out of EMU could have a beneficial effect on Danish bonds.

A common European currency could reduce opportunities for currency speculation, encouraging a flow of speculative funds into Denmark, narrowing spreads between Danish bonds and their European counterparts, they said.
